parts:
2 - 
This is more of a general modeling question, but I cannot seem to find any guidance here so I'm going to throw it out there. If the global model is one of the top models (Delta AIC <4) is that bad? My adviser seems to think so, but I can't find good guidelines or discussion on this or why that would be. I understand why having the null in the top models would be troubling, but not why the global model (the model including all the covariates being considered) would be troublesome. Feel free to just point me towards a book or a paper or whatever. I think I've reached the end of my self-taught modeller rope. 


Auriel

Imagine a candidate set of models: null (dot) models at one end (no temporal/spatial variation in anything), and fully time-dependent models at the other (imagine a t subscript for anything looking vaguely lke some Greek-letter-cum-parameter).  In the middle, you have some models where the variation over space or time is constrained to be a function of one or more 'covariates of interest'. 

Given this 'continuum', then you could make the following rather dry observations:

1\ if the null model is the 'best' by various criterion, then your data are too sparse (or insufficient wrt model structure) to make any sort of interesting inference. A null model has no biological meaning, since there is no parameter outside of physics which is truly a constant over space time. So, a null model doesn't mean 'no temporal variation', it means 'your data set is insufficient to detect the variation that must be there, at least to some degree'.

2\ if the general model comes out on top, relative to your covariate models, then this is a different sort of problem. A fully general model indicates heterogeneity over time or space (or both), but, variation that isn't explained is meaningless white noise (and yes, even if you're estimating process variance for a PVA or some such, simply unexplained variation around a mean is a pretty naive estimator for process variance). Temporal or spatial variation in and of itself is *not* interesting. What *is* interesting is what 'drives' the variation. In most ecology, the drive-response sequence is 'inferred'. Meaning, unless we do an experiment, we're left with what JD Nichols calls 'post hoc story telling'. At the least, though, we can strive to tell interesting stories. So, if your general model wins, and does better than your covariate-constrained models (each of which is in effect 'a story'), then all you can conclude is that you're not a good story teller. More 'gently', it implies that your covariate set aren't particularly informative. 

So, if you have a some degree of lack of resolution among the 'general' model and the 'covariate' models, then you have litytle basis for infering tat the covariates do much of anything. The fact that your general model does better than the null model means your data are at least sufficient to support that distinction. But failing to differentiate the general and covariate models is less a 'data' problem (at least, not directly), but is more a problem in terms of thinking hard about meaningful covariates. So, in response to Andy, I would submit that this is a 'problem', at least to some extent -- if the intent is to tell good stories. If the intent is driven by estimator parsimony, then if you average over the models, it won't make a lot of difference. 

As for the whole delta AIC <4  or 2, or any of those sorts of rules of thumb, I would argue they're not particularly useful. If you're working with likelihood-based methods, then far better to use evidence ratios. You might want to have a look at section 4.4.1 in chapter 4 of the MARK book (marked or unmarked, the principles are the same): http://www.phidot.org/software/mark/docs/book/pdf/chap4.pdf

messages.subject: Re: density vs abund & the ranking of global models
parts:
Evan, this problem is only relevant if a general model is in the model set.  And it would seem more commonly applicable to the detection model structure than to that of the state process.  Rarely are folks fitting models in unmarked that include a global model that is completely general, given that space is typically the dimension of most interest.  I don't think anybody is fitting models with the spatial replicate as a fixed effect - you can try it and watch the AIC drop, but as you said the inferences are useless.  If one's interest is in time, you either have an impressive time series that can actually examine covariates in that dimension, or you are modeling the detection process (where the combined time and space replication gives you more power).  And if your most general detection model turns out to be best, while not ideal, I doubt you are losing sleep about the story telling.

Just wanted to point out that this problem is probably not pervasive for unmarked users.  And I could easily see someone confusing the relevance of a general vs. global model in the interpretation of top models (especially when advocating rules of thumb).

Evan, remember that I'm referring to situations typical of models in unmarked here.  Site is the common sampling unit, replicated over space (and sometimes time).  I don't see how it makes any sense to fit a general model where every site has its own fixed effect.  Obviously such a model would be way over-parameterized, but it would certainly provide a good fit.  I guess I don't understand what exactly you mean by a general model here.  For example, what does the "general model" look like for a typical occupancy model?

As for 25 years of real birds, yeah that's a nice data set.  I suppose with fake birds you could have 1,000+ years of data, so it's a tradeoff!

Regarding the utility of a general detection model, if you are estimating a single N with capture-recapture then yes, your detection model plays a prominent role and may be most important to the story telling.  But as I said earlier, unmarked models are seeking to make inference on variation in N across sites or time.  That is the variation most important to the story telling, at least for those models.

messages.author: 0227543d81e2924c
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Re: density vs abund & the ranking of global models
parts:
The general model (as understood by the *many* people who use that phrase -- some of them named Burnham, and Anderson, and so on) is the most parameterized model in the candidate model set. Since all parameters vary over space and time, then the usual starting point is to have a general model with time/space dependence in those parameters. if the data set is insufficient to fit to that model, then the general model is occasional a reduced parameter for of same, at least for some parameters. The assumption is that the general model adequately fits the data. Fit of all other models is scaled relative to that. Thats fundamental to GOF testing (where the general model is an approximation to a saturated model, which can't be specified for most data types), multi-model inference, and any number of things.

So, the distinction (which you could argue is semantic, although most of the estimation world refers to the most parameterized model as 'the general model') is made because it represents a point on the continuum for the candidate model set. Because it is general, it will fit, but have no explanatory power. That power comes from the comparison of other reduced models to the general model. if your gneral model is the best fitting, then you eally don't know anything other than the fact that you have 'variation', which is not particular informative (since variation at some level is a give).
On 3/11/2015 12:43 PM, Dan Linden wrote:

If your definition of a general model is one where parameters are time-specific, why is time not simply considered a covariate like any other?  I agree that if time explains important variation in parameters, by itself the interpretation is of questionable value.  I just don't see why the "general model" distinction needs to be made.

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Re: density vs abund & the ranking of global models
parts:
Evan, to be clear I'm not questioning your expertise on this subject.  In the words of Wayne and Garth: "We're not worthy!"  To some extent I'm playing devil's advocate precisely because of the semantics.  And for this discussion to be useful to others, particularly the users of unmarked, sometimes things need to be described in the fullest detail.

So we've got a general model, a global model, and a saturated model.  FWIW, Burnham & Anderson (2002) mention them all but have an index entry only for "global model".  It is true they are all the same thing, conditional on a candidate model set - simply, the most parameterized model.  But unconditionally, the definitions of most parameterized model can differ, namely in that folks may disagree on what qualifies as most parameterized.  This was largely my point.

Theoretically, the most parameterized model contains a parameter for every single data point.  By every data point I mean the product of replicates across all sampled dimensions (e.g., for simple occupancy: sites*surveys).  This model fits perfectly but has no explanatory power.  Realistically, it cannot actually be fit for many model structures, particularly latent variable models.  Evan, you said that if the data set is insufficient, the general model is occasionally a reduced parameter model.  I would argue that, for applications relevant to unmarked and often elsewhere, it is ALWAYS a reduced parameter model.  B&A talk about selecting the global model to represent the most reasonably complex parameterization, which is different than being the theoretically most parameterized.

Therefore, if the theoretically most parameterized model is never actually the general model in a candidate set, then it is confusing to say that the general model has no explanatory power (at least in practice).  This is why I don't think having the general/global/saturated model as your best model is ever a problem.  Evan, you explained why Auriel may have received the concerns that she did.  I just wanted to further clarify why such concerns are not generally applicable to unmarked users.

parts:
On 3/11/2015 3:58 PM, Dan Linden wrote:

So we've got a general model, a global model, and a saturated model.
General and global are the same thing, in practice.

FWIW, Burnham & Anderson (2002) mention them all but have an index entry only for "global model".

It is true they are all the same thing, conditional on a candidate model set - simply, the most parameterized model.  But unconditionally, the definitions of most parameterized model can differ, namely in that folks may disagree on what qualifies as most parameterized.  This was largely my point.

Uh, most parameterized means...most parameters. Kind of hard to be ambiguous about that. Now, what constitutes effective sample size, different issue. But the parameter space is not the basis for a disagreement. The model with the most parameters is the most general model.
Theoretically, the most parameterized model contains a parameter for every single data point.
Said model being saturated, but not always plausible to build it. There are a lot of data types for which the saturatred model isn't known.
By every data point I mean the product of replicates across all sampled dimensions (e.g., for simple occupancy: sites*surveys).  This model fits perfectly but has no explanatory power.
Agreed. But it isn't the general approximating model I'm referring to, as I suspect you know. If I meant the saturated model, I would have said so.
Realistically, it cannot actually be fit for many model structures, particularly latent variable models.
yes, as everyone should know already.

Evan, you said that if the data set is insufficient, the general model is occasionally a reduced parameter model.  I would argue that, for applications relevant to unmarked and often elsewhere, it is ALWAYS a reduced parameter model.

Reduced relative to the saturated model. But thats not a model you include in your candidate model set. The whole discussion is based on models you build in your candidate model set. Nothing more. In said model set, you have (or should) a general model, that is sufficiently parameterized to adequately fit the data.
B&A talk about selecting the global model to represent the most reasonably complex parameterization, which is different than being the theoretically most parameterized.
No kidding.

Therefore, if the theoretically most parameterized model is never actually the general model in a candidate set, then it is confusing to say that the general model has no explanatory power (at least in practice).  This is why I don't think having the general/global/saturated model as your best model is ever a problem.

This is where I think you're wrong. If your general model -- time variation in lots of parameters -- is your best model, you have learned....nothing. Showing that a model that has variation over time or space in a parameter is not informative. *Why* there is variation is the point of the exercise.

So, yes, if your best model is the general model in a candidate model set, then you have a problem. This isn't a nuance that is more or less relevant for unmarked, or anything else.
Evan, you explained why Auriel may have received the concerns that she did.  I just wanted to further clarify why such concerns are not generally applicable to unmarked users.

And, I think you're giving her erroneous advice. Your argument (that the general model is not the theoretically most general) applies to *all* modeling, marked or otherwise. A model that does no more than allow for unspecific heterogeneity over space or time is not a useful model, in and of itself. Its utility lies in the contrast of that model with other models in the candidate model set. It is a reference model, not a model for informative inference.

p(t+temp) isn't a valid model, since you shouldn't include a temporally varying environmental covariate in a time dependent model. In fact, that is sufficiently egregious that Gary makes it the the first of the 10 MARK commandments:  to quote "Thou shalt not use a temporally varying covariate with a fully time varying model". That would be your model (4).

2) p(t)
3) p(temp)

I agree.
Which would you say is the global model?  Which is the "general model" to which you keep referring?
2. It has more parameters. Model 3 has 2 for a parameter: intercept, plus beta for temp. Model 2 has intercept, plus n-1 columns in the design matrix
If #4 is your best model, have you learned nothing?

Well, if (4) is your best model, you've learned nothing because it isn't a valid model.

So, let's be specific -- if (2) was the best model, then no, you haven't learned anything. If (2) was the best model -- then you have.

Would having #4 as the best be a problem?  How have your comments thus far clarified any of this?

A model that does no more than allow for unspecific heterogeneity over space or time is not a useful model, in and of itself.

Sure, and this would be model #2 in my example.  Are you saying this is the global model?
Correct, for the reason I specified.

If not, what exactly is your point?  My point has been that having the global model as the best model is not typically a problem.  You seem to be suggesting that it is a problem when the global model is one that only has unspecified heterogeneity in time or space.  I don't disagree with that.  I disagree with the contention that this is a commonly used global model, at least for applications of unmarked.

Once more, then I'm done. If the general model is unspecificed time-varying data, then it is not informative.  Your example (model 4) is not a valid linear model if time is a factorial element of the model (it might be if time is entered as a trend), so given models (1) -> (3) are valid, then even if model (3) has all the support in the data among the candidate models, I haven't really learned much. You might say that I've learned that p(temp) isn't a good model, and I've learned that temp isn't a good predictor. Which was my original point. having a general time-dependent model with all the support, relative to the models with covariates, teaches you only that those aren't good predictors of the variation. But, it isn't informative in telling anything about what does drive the variation.

messages.author: 527d9b3ec7deff2d
messages.subject: Re: density vs abund & the ranking of global models
parts:
Evan, I never presumed you didn't know what you were talking about.  That is why I made the Wayne's World comment - you are clearly an expert, there is no question.  I apologize for implying otherwise.  My intention was to focus the discussion because there are some differences with respect to the types of models fit in programs like PRESENCE and unmarked, vs. those typically fit in MARK (with some heavy overlap).  I know that you know all of this, again my comments are always with respect to unmarked users.

Convenient for the sake of our discussion, we both approached my simple example from different angles.  I was not at all clear, but I envisioned the temperature covariate to be something that varied by time and space.  This is a typical situation where site is the sampling unit, as in an occupancy model.  It certainly does not apply when individual is the sampling unit, as in a mark-recapture model.  That critical detail makes all the difference here.

So much of this material can be very confusing to the average user.  And it is hard to balance advocating rules of thumb vs. discouraging folks from relying on analysis recipes that sometimes lead to misguided decisions.  I guess what you hope is that people adequately familiarize themselves with the literature and seek expert opinions when possible.

My intention was to run them using the output=density, but when I do I get the heissian is singular error (my least favorite unmarked error). if I change output to output=abund, it works fine, no error. This raises a read flag to me, but I wasn't sure if it actually should, thoughts?

2 - 
This is more of a general modeling question, but I cannot seem to find any guidance here so I'm going to throw it out there. If the global model is one of the top models (Delta AIC <4) is that bad? My adviser seems to think so, but I can't find good guidelines or discussion on this or why that would be. I understand why having the null in the top models would be troubling, but not why the global model (the model including all the covariates being considered) would be troublesome. Feel free to just point me towards a book or a paper or whatever. I think I've reached the end of my self-taught modeller rope. 


Auriel

messages.subject: Re: density vs abund & the ranking of global models
parts:
Hi Dan,
As a novice unmarked user (and novice at modeling in general), this conversation was *slightly* hard for me to follow, so I just want to confirm what was settled on:

If I have an sample model set:
1) occu(~1~1, data=data) #null model
2) occu(~%cover+trailtype+humanactivity+month~1, data=data) #global model
3) occu(~%cover+trailtype~1, data=data) #subglobal
4) occu(~%cover+month~1, data=data) #subglobal
etc etc...

...and if model 2 (global model) was ranked as the top model with AIC( chat ~1), then I haven't learned anything, correct? 

Does this mean that there is variation in my data that isn't explained by my covariates?
...I'm just having a hard time interpreting this and figuring what I need to do to fix my models so that they are meaningful!

I appreciate your help, your comments are always very useful for me!!

On Wednesday, March 11, 2015 at 9:47:35 PM UTC-4, Dan Linden wrote:
Evan, I never presumed you didn't know what you were talking about.  That is why I made the Wayne's World comment - you are clearly an expert, there is no question.  I apologize for implying otherwise.  My intention was to focus the discussion because there are some differences with respect to the types of models fit in programs like PRESENCE and unmarked, vs. those typically fit in MARK (with some heavy overlap).  I know that you know all of this, again my comments are always with respect to unmarked users.

Convenient for the sake of our discussion, we both approached my simple example from different angles.  I was not at all clear, but I envisioned the temperature covariate to be something that varied by time and space.  This is a typical situation where site is the sampling unit, as in an occupancy model.  It certainly does not apply when individual is the sampling unit, as in a mark-recapture model.  That critical detail makes all the difference here.

So much of this material can be very confusing to the average user.  And it is hard to balance advocating rules of thumb vs. discouraging folks from relying on analysis recipes that sometimes lead to misguided decisions.  I guess what you hope is that people adequately familiarize themselves with the literature and seek expert opinions when possible.

messages.author: 527d9b3ec7deff2d
messages.subject: Re: density vs abund & the ranking of global models
parts:
So glad to see this old thread resurrected.  :-D

To clarify, Carly, your example does not suggest you've learned nothing.  It also does not suggest unexplained variation, as far as I can tell.  A few thoughts:

1) I recommend Andy and Marc's AHM book for a very accessible treatment on occupancy in unmarked and hierarchical modeling in general: Applied Hiearchical Modeling in Ecology

2) To be clear, all covariates in your example are detection covariates.  So you haven't learned anything about variation in occupancy there.  If your objectives relate to the detection process for some species, particularly if you are designing future monitoring, and/or you have no reason to think there is spatial variation in occurrence, this could make sense.

3) I stand by my comments that having the global model rank as the top model in an occupancy analysis is not a "problem".  I am certainly open to being shown otherwise.  This thread highlights nuance that goes way beyond occupancy or the unmarked package.

messages.subject: Re: density vs abund & the ranking of global models
parts:
Hi all,

I thought I'd resurrect this thread. I'm currently facing a similar situation to what Auriel and Carly experienced. In ranking a set of single season occupancy models that just include covariates of detection, the most general model was the top ranked one. This seems to be a fairly uncommon situation, as I haven't found other cases of people describing this issue on the internet. 

From this thread, I've gathered that a general model being lowest-ranked in AIC might signal that the covariates being considered aren't informative.

Does anyone else have an opinion to add to Dan and Evan's discussion here, or know of any papers that describe this pattern and its cause in more detail? 


Cheers,
David
